title: arXiv AI papers — Friday, 13 November 2026
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart, so this ordering is inferred from checkable attention and quality signals plus relevance; the papers are very recent and Semantic Scholar listed zero current citations for these selected records at the snapshot, so popularity cannot be established.

sections.title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
sections.abstract: The authors introduce CRAM, a learned Hopfield–Tank energy for constraint puzzles, reporting near-perfect Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique accuracy with at least 1,000× faster training and 282× fewer inference FLOPs than looped baselines on the studied tasks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The paper trains an explicit energy directly from solved puzzles and reports fast, data-efficient reasoning on Sudoku, maze, N-Queens, and graph-coloring tasks (arXiv abstract and paper discussion).
sections.unique_caveat: The authors caution that these constraint puzzles are unusually well matched to CRAM’s pairwise energy and that high scores do not establish scalability to harder tasks such as ARC-AGI; learning the latent quantities needed for harder reasoning remains open (paper discussion).
sections.ranking_evidence: The clearest independent technical discussion found for this batch is Ken Ashe’s 13 November analysis; the authors also provide a public CRAM repository. These are visible discussion and artifact signals, not readership statistics.

sections.title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
sections.abstract: AgentSSL frames semi-supervised learning as agentic program search and reports that generated pipelines outperform human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings, while program selection can lose as much as 47% when guided by the agent’s feedback metric.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors formulate semi-supervised learning as agentic search over executable SSL programs and release ProgramSelectBench to evaluate choosing among candidate programs (arXiv abstract and paper text).
sections.unique_caveat: The authors report that on both ecology tasks the supervised AgentSL variant matches AgentSSL, describe their search as biased toward SSL, and call reliable program selection without labels unresolved (paper discussion).
sections.ranking_evidence: Listed as a NeurIPS 2026 poster and cross-listed in two core AI categories; the paper introduces a substantial 16,977-program selection benchmark. The conference listing is a quality signal, not a popularity measure.

sections.title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
sections.abstract: The paper formalizes settings where a verifier can reliably reject failures but cannot certify apparent successes, and proposes NOPO, which updates a policy by suppressing trusted negatives rather than rewarding unverified positives.
sections.claimed_contribution: NOPO combines reference-relative suppression of verifier-negative samples with a group-level weight based on non-falsified alternatives; the authors report pass@k gains across code, logic, and math evaluations with unit-test, constraint, and LLM-based verifiers (abstract and paper conclusion).
sections.unique_caveat: The authors state that negative-only learning identifies what to avoid but not where the removed probability mass should go; their conservative update is intended to limit this problem, while exploiting partial positive evidence remains future work (paper limitations).
sections.ranking_evidence: The arXiv record identifies the paper as a NeurIPS 2026 Spotlight; it is cross-listed in two core AI categories. The spotlight status is a conference signal, not a direct measure of readership.

sections.title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
sections.abstract: Using counterfactual substitutions in retrieved passages, the authors estimate that some cited claims come from a model’s parametric memory rather than the retrieved context, and find that standard natural-language-inference checks do not reliably identify this provenance mismatch.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors propose counterfactual value substitution to distinguish facts retrieved from context from facts supplied by parametric memory, and compare ten attribution methods (arXiv abstract).
sections.unique_caveat: The authors say their best detector is not accurate enough to act on: it measures what a model knows rather than what it actually used. The reported model set spans five sizes from one family and one comparator family (abstract).
sections.ranking_evidence: The paper received multiple recent third-party explainers, including Learn AI Visually and Bharat Hunt, giving it more visible outside discussion than most papers in the batch. These explainers are attention signals only, not evidence that the method is validated.

sections.title: LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds
sections.abstract: The authors introduce GeoWorld and LiveGeo, a controllable geographic environment and benchmark where agents must acquire relevant evidence, check whether it remains valid as the world changes, and revise decisions; their tests find that strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability.
sections.claimed_contribution: GeoWorld provides evolving, verifiable geographic state histories, while LiveGeo tests information gathering, evidence revalidation, and replanning in that environment (arXiv abstract).
sections.unique_caveat: The evidence is specific to the proposed geographic benchmark and tasks; the abstract does not establish reliability in other dynamic environments or real-world deployments.
sections.ranking_evidence: Two recent secondary write-ups discuss the benchmark, alongside the arXiv release. This is a modest external-attention signal; the paper has no cross-list breadth among the core AI categories.

sections.title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
sections.abstract: CoReMem values memory by testing its effect on subsequent repository tasks and adapts coding agents to use it; on ChainSWE, the authors report higher resolution rate and fewer steps and cache-aware tokens for a 27B actor than the untrained actor without memory.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce prospective segment valuation and provenance-gated memory credit, using these to build compact repository memories and adapt an actor to use them (arXiv abstract).
sections.unique_caveat: The abstract reports one benchmark (ChainSWE) and one 27B actor comparison; it does not establish that the memory strategy transfers to other repositories, agents, or task distributions.
sections.ranking_evidence: It spans three core AI categories and reports task-resolution and token-use outcomes on a coding-agent benchmark. No independent attention signal was evident in the sources checked, so it is included as a relevant new result rather than treated as a popularity leader.

sections.title: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
sections.abstract: Metal Sandbox combines restricted per-agent workspaces, native macOS command execution, and scheduling across Macs; four Mac mini M4 tests and replayed agent traces report throughput gains and lower tool waiting under the stated workloads.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors combine per-instance file isolation, command-level scheduling, and migration of eligible waiting commands between Macs; their abstract reports 1.68×–2.05× throughput in concentrated-demand tests and reductions in waiting and batch time in trace replay.
sections.unique_caveat: The sustained-throughput estimate assumes continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean command durations; its evaluation is on four Macs and does not establish behavior under different hardware or workload mixes (abstract).
sections.ranking_evidence: The paper is cross-listed across three core AI categories plus distributed computing and links public Metal Sandbox and Harbor repositories. The breadth and released code make it a useful systems result; they are not evidence of high readership.

sections.title: When Both Sides Adapt: The Challenges of Evaluating Interactive LLM Systems
sections.abstract: The paper distinguishes model comparisons on a shared prompt distribution from comparisons on the prompts users generate in response to each model, showing that offline benchmarks and live A/B tests can estimate different effects and sometimes reverse model rankings.
sections.claimed_contribution: The author defines common- and induced-distribution effects, establishes which standard estimators target them, characterizes ranking reversals, and gives a sufficient condition for rankings to agree (arXiv abstract).
sections.unique_caveat: The variance result is derived in a stylized linear interaction model, while the paper notes that measuring prompt composition and task-level behavior can be difficult in high-dimensional general-purpose LLM settings (abstract and discussion).
sections.ranking_evidence: The cross-list bridges statistical methodology and AI, and the paper gives a formal account of when offline and interactive evaluations diverge. No independent attention signal was evident in the sources checked, so this is retained for relevance rather than asserted popularity.
